newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK activists return to heroes' welcome from isles.
newsitem.headline: HK activists return to heroes' welcome from isles.

text.p: Activists returned to a heroes' welcome in Hong Kong on Tuesday after hoisting Chinese flags on a disputed group of islands in the East China Sea.
Hundreds of well-wishers applauded as the 84 activists arrived at Hong Kong's Kai Tak airport to be reunited with friends and family.
In the arrival hall, girls placed garlands around the activists' necks, while outside a crowd of more than 100 people unfurled banners.
"A triumphant return! A safe return! A victorious return! Protect national territory! Protect the Diaoyu islands!" they chanted.

On Monday, together with Taiwan campaigners, the activists pierced a Japanese maritime cordon, went ashore on one of the islands and hoisted the flags of China and Taiwan's exiled Republic of China in a bid to assert China's sovereignty over the rocky outcrops.
Japan, which calls the islands the Senkakus, has claimed sovereign rights to them and refused to acknowledge that the dispute is still open for discussion with China.
Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over what it calls the Diaoyus for centuries.
"We had a group of united members," Chan Yu-nam, who planted a Chinese flag on the islet, said.
Another activist burst into tears when telling of the group's failure to demolish a lighthouse erected by Japanese right-wingers on the islands.

Team leader Albert Ho said he regreted the failure, and urged Chinese all over the world to support China's claims to the islands. He also urged China's and Taiwan's governments to take positive measures on their claims to sovereignty.
"Problems and disputes among Chinese can be put aside. The more important thing is to reclaim our territory and fight against Japanese militarists," he said.
The activists observed a moment's silence for David Chan, a campaigner who drowned late last month in a similar protest voyage to the islands.
Activist Chan Yu-nam offered a bouquet to David Chan's eldest sister, Chan Lai-ying, who hailed the group's efforts at the airport.

"Yesterday, when I heard that our compatriots landed on the Diaoyu islands and had placed a flag there, the entire family felt very excited and encouraged. David's sacrifice was worthwhile," she said.
Ho said the group would push for economic and political sanctions against Japan, but stressed the move was aimed at Japanese militarism and not at Japanese in general.
